Source and Chemistry

Table from slide 2
Heparin Warfarin
Natural sulfated polysaccharide present in mast cells

Carries negative charge

Commercial preparations are derived from bovine lung or porcine intestinal extracts and there is synthetic ones 		- Synthetic coumarin compound

Pharmacokinetics

Table from slide 3
Heparin Warfarin
Absorption It can’t be absorbed by the GIT because it gets precipitated by the gastric HCL It can be absorbed and it is well absorbed with 100% bioavailability
Available formulas IV and SC Oral only
Distribution Cannot pass cross BBB or placenta Can cross both BBB and placenta

Mechanism of action

Before we explain the mechanism of action for these medications, first we have to understand some vital points about the coagulation cascade:

  • Unfractionated heparin works by activating the antithrombin III (natural clotting inhibitor available in plasma)
  • Antithrombin III work to inhibit several clotting factors especially factor X and factor II
  • Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase enzyme in the liver leading to inhibition of the formation of the active form of vitamin K
  • This will lead to inhibition of the synthesis of vitamin K dependent clotting factors (X, IX, VII, and II)
  • The action of warfarin can be antagonized by vit K

Onset and duration of clinical effects

Table from slide 8
Heparin Warfarin
Rapid onset of action if given IV, and onset in 1-2 hours if given SC

It has short duration (2-4 hours) 		Delayed onset of action 24-72 hours after administration, this is the time needed for depletion of vit k and vit k dependent clotting factors

Long duration of action (2- 5 days), until the liver produce the depleted vit K and coagulation factors

Pharmacological effects

Table from slide 9
Heparin Warfarin
Anticoagulation in vivo and in vitro

Stimulates lipoprotein lipase which lead to decrease serum triglycerides 		Anticoagulation in vivo only

Therapeutic uses

Table from slide 10
Heparin Warfarin
Heparin is indicated for prevention and treatment of thrombotic events (to prevent thrombus propagation in established thrombosis) such as DVT, PE, AF, ACS; it can also be used to prevent coagulation during cardiac surgery, PCI, extracorporeal circulation and dialysis

Dosing is variable but it is common to start with a bolus dose of 80 units/Kg IV then maintained by 18 units/kg/h; Dosing in ACS and stroke is much lower because there is higher risk of bleeding 		Warfarin is indicated for prophylaxis and treatment (treatment means prevent thrombus propagation in established thrombosis) of DVT, PE, AF or cardiac valve replacement

Warfarin is also indicated in reduction in risk of death in recurrent MI, and thromboembolic events (e.g. stroke, systemic embolization) after MI

Given orally 2- 10 mg/day

Monitoring of therapy

Table from slide 11
Heparin Warfarin
By activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)

APTT checked at baseline and then every 6 hours until 2 or more therapeutic values are obtained then it is checked every 24 hours

Dose titration is according to the APTT

Monitoring for adverse effects includes Hb, hematocrit (bleeding), PLT and vital signs 		By prothrombin time (PT) or international normalized ratio (INR)

INR is preferred over PT

INR value in patient without anticoagulation is 1

INR is monitored serially until the required therapeutic value is reached

Adverse effects

Table from slide 12
Heparin Warfarin
Bleeding: very dangerous, e.g. intracranial hemorrhage, GI bleeding, intraocular bleeding, hemarthrosis…
bleeding could be treated with:
Immediate stopping of the medication
Fresh frozen plasma: to replace the clotting factors
Protamine sulfate: protamine carries a positive charge that bind to the heparin which have a negative charge to form a stable complex; 1 mg of protamine can bind to 100 U of heparin
Bleeding: very dangerous, e.g. intracranial hemorrhage, GI bleeding, intraocular bleeding, hemarthrosis…
bleeding could be treated with:
Immediate stopping of the medication
Fresh frozen plasma: to replace the clotting factors
Vitamin K: 10 mg slowly IV or IM to enhance synthesis of clotting factors
Table from slide 13
Heparin Warfarin
Heparin can’t be given IM but if it is given , it will lead to hematoma formation

Thrombocytopenia: there are 2 types of thrombocytopenia associated with heparin use, the first type is non immunogenic interaction with PLT that occur within the first 48-72 hours of initiation of heparin therapy, this is temporary drop in PLT and will recover once heparin is stopped; the second type is much more serious known as heparin induced thrombocytopenia and this is immune mediated reactions against PLT occur 5 days after heparin initiation and it can lead to thrombosis e.g. PE, DVT, stroke , MI… (HITT)
Warfarin may also lead to GI side effects like nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain

Hemorrhagic skin necrosis: when starting warfarin, biosynthesis of protein C is reduced leading to temporary procoagulant state. This can lead to hemorrhagic infarction of skin, breast, intestine and fatty tissue. Normally avoided by concurrent heparin administration

Purple toe syndrome: characterized by cholesterol microembolization that causes purple lesions to develop on the toes and sides of feet
Table from slide 14
Heparin Warfarin
Other heparin adverse effects include hyperkalemia, alopecia and osteoporosis (with long term use)
Teratogenicity: abnormal bone formation in early pregnancy (fetal warfarin syndrome)

CNS hemorrhage in the fetus if given in late pregnancy

Sudden withdrawal may lead to thrombotic catastrophes

Anticoagulants contraindications

  • PLT count < 100 000
  • Active, uncontrollable bleeding except for DIC
  • Patient has a history of heparin induced thrombocytopenia can’t be given heparin
  • Routine monitoring tests can’t be performed for any reason
  • Threatened abortion, eclampsia or preeclampsia
